5.5.2 Potential Energy: Potential energy (P.E) is defined as the energy stored in an object due to its position relative to other objects or its configuration. It is a form of mechanical energy and can be converted into kinetic energy (the energy of motion) or other forms of energy.

Fig 5.4: A concept of P.E The compressed string, a catapult about to set, a body at certain height above the ground are said to have P.E. If a body is raised to a height h above the ground surface against gravitational pull, then work done, w = f.h = mgh = gain in P.E. P.E. = mgh, is the gravitational P.E Examples: i) A stretched rubber or a compressed spring possesses P.E. ii) A bent bow possesses P.E. iii) A compressed gas possesses P.E. iv) Water in a dam anda ball raised to height have gravitational P.E. of primary focus.

Facts on K.E. &P. E. Finally, we write, K.E. + P.E. =Total mechanical energy If K.E is maximum, P.E is zero and vice versa. i) A man resting on his bed has potential energy (P.E.), while a man running at his top speed possesses only kinetic energy (K.E.). A man, walking normally, possesses a combination of kinetic energy and potential energy, with a portion being kinetic and the remainder being potential. ii) The water in a pond does possess potential energy (P.E.), and the distribution of this pond water to an urban area involves the transformation of potential energy into kinetic energy (K.E.).

iii) The energy stored in a stretched string is potential energy (P.E.). When a stone is released from such a string, as in a catapult, there is a conversion of this potential energy into kinetic energy (K.E.). iv) The release of the arrow from a stretched bow exemplifies the transformation of potential energy (P.E.) into kinetic energy (K.E.). v) When the compressed gas in a bicycle tire bursts, the potential energy stored in the compressed gas is transformed into kinetic energy and other forms of energy such as sound and heat. A body can possess potential energy (PE) due to its positional state but may not have momentum. Furthermore, a body with no energy also has no momentum.

Fig 5.5 Variation of KE and PE What about the concept of change in PE = work done by/against a force? Worked Out Examples: Q 5.5 A mass of 10Kg is taken from the ground for 10m uphill on the wedge. The wedge makes an angle of 30° with the ground. Find the potential energy of the block. Solution: Here, mass, m = 10 kg Length of the wedge, L = 10m Angle of inclination of the wedge with the ground, θ = 300 We have, P.E = mgh= 10 × 10 × h = 100x Lsin300 = 100× 10× 1 = 500 joule.

Sample Question: 1. Water is pumped vertically upwards through a distance of 100m and the work done is 294 kilo joule. Calculate the volume of the water pumped. (Given density of water = 103 kg/m3) (Ans: 2.94 × 10-5 m3.) 5.6 Principle of Conservation of Energy We have studied different forms of energy in our previous classes. These include mechanical energy, heat energy, sound energy, chemical energy, light energy, electrical energy, and so on. When one form of energy disappears, the next form of energy is evolved, and vice versa. There is no destruction or creation of energy; it only changes its form.

i) When we turn on a radio, the chemical energy in the battery or the electrical energy supplied is converted into sound energy. Here, the loss of the former type of energy is balanced by the production of the second kind of energy. ii) When a fan is turned on, the electrical energy supplied is converted into mechanical energy. The amount of electrical energy expended is balanced by the generation of mechanical energy. In summary, the principle of conservation of energy can be stated as: “Energy can neither be created nor be destroyed, but it can be changed from one form to another form” iii) The principle of conservation of energy is an empirical principle and cannot be proved purely through mathematics. iv) The law is also believed to be universally valid, as it has not been contradicted in any experiment or observation of nature. v) The law connects mechanics to all other branches of physics, making the concept of energy one of the unifying ideas of physics. vi) The mechanical energy is conserved only when the forces are conservative in nature. vii) The energy spent against the friction dissipates in the form of heat energy which isn’t available for useful work.
The conservation of energy is best understood by taking the example of a pendulum motion.
